AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: This study investigated the associations of subjectively and objectively measured physical activity (PA) and sedentary behavior with academic achievement. We further examined whether aerobic fitness, obesity, and bedtime mediate these associations.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: This study included 970 children aged 9-15 (52.3% girls) from nine schools throughout Finland. Register-based academic achievement (grade point average [GPA]) as well as self-reported and accelerometer-measured PA/sedentary behavior were assessed during spring 2013. Aerobic fitness, assessed via a maximal shuttle run test, body composition assessed via bioimpedance analysis, and self-reported bedtime were collected. Structural equation modelling was applied to examine the associations. Standardized regression coefficients are presented.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Self-reported PA had a direct positive (β=0.084, 95% confidence interval [CI]=0.023-0.145) and an indirect positive association with GPA through higher aerobic fitness (β=0.061, CI=0.033-0.087). Accelerometer-based PA was not associated with GPA. Self-reported screen time had an indirect negative association with GPA through later bedtime (β=-0.071, CI=-0.096--0.035) and lower aerobic fitness (β=-0.039, CI=-0.059--0.019). Non-screen sedentary time had a direct positive (β=0.193, CI=0.101-0.289) and an indirect negative association with GPA through lower aerobic fitness (β=-0.040, CI=-0.063--0.016).

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Participating in PA, avoiding excessive screen time, and going to bed earlier may benefit academic achievement.
